steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual picture (zooming out first, then in)

1. What problem are we solving?  
   We want a model that, given a sequence of symbols (words, sub-words, pixels, amino acids, …), can (a) build a rich internal representation of the whole sequence and (b) emit a new sequence (translation, continuation, answer) one step at a time.  
   Key requirements:
   • See every part of the sequence, not just neighbors.  
   • Decide which parts matter for the current decision.  
   • Run fast on modern hardware (parallel, GPU-friendly).

2. The central idea: “Let every token look at every other token and ask: how relevant are you to me right now?”  
   This is called attention. Mathematically it boils down to a soft lookup table: similarity scores → softmax → weighted average of information from the other tokens. Because every token can consult every other token in one matrix operation, the computation is parallel.

3. Building blocks of a Transformer layer  
   a. Input embeddings: Each token is mapped to a vector.  
   b. Positional information: Add or concatenate a position signal so the model knows order.  
   c. Self-attention: For each token we form three vectors—Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V)—by multiplying the embedding with learned weight matrices.  
      • Dot products Q·Kᵀ give pairwise relevance scores.  
      • Scale and soft-max over the keys so the scores become probabilities.  
      • Use them to blend (“attend to”) the Value vectors; result = a context vector for that token.  
   d. Multi-head trick: Do the above several times in parallel with different learned weights. Each head can focus on a different kind of relation (syntax, agreement, topic, …). Concatenate the heads and linearly mix them.  
   e. Feed-forward network: A small MLP applied to every position separately (same weights for all positions).  
   f. Add & Norm: After both the attention block and the feed-forward block we add the input (residual connection) and normalize (LayerNorm). This stabilizes gradients and lets the layer learn “adjustments” rather than a full rewrite.

   One such “Attention → Add&Norm → Feed-Forward → Add&Norm” unit is a Transformer block. Stack 6, 12, 24, … of them and you have an encoder (BERT) or decoder (GPT) or both (original Transformer for translation).

4. Encoder, decoder, or both?  
   Encoder: processes the entire input in parallel. Each block is a self-attention block. Output = contextualized embeddings. Good for inspection tasks (classification, retrieval, etc.).  
   Decoder: generates tokens one by one. Every layer has (1) masked self-attention (can only look at past positions), (2) encoder-decoder attention (looks at encoder outputs), (3) feed-forward. Good for generation.  
   The original “Transformer” paper (Vaswani et al., 2017) had an encoder and a decoder; GPT keeps only the decoder; BERT keeps only the encoder but asks it to predict masked words.

5. Putting it to work  
   • Training objective: usually cross-entropy to make the predicted distribution over next/ masked/ target tokens match ground truth.  
   • Gradients flow through attention just like through dense layers. Because attention is a matrix of differentiable softmax weights, the model learns which patterns to emphasize.  
   • Everything sits in big matrices; GPUs eat matrices for breakfast → huge speed-ups compared with recurrent nets.

6. Why is it effective?  
   • Global context: Any token can directly influence any other token in one step. Long-range dependencies are no longer filtered through many recurrent hops.  
   • Interpretability: You can inspect the attention weights to see which tokens looked at which.  
   • Scalability: Complexity per layer is O(L²) in sequence length L but independent of hidden width, and no temporal recursion → easy to parallelize across time dimension.  
   • Flexibility: Same backbone works for language, vision, audio, protein folding, etc., just change the embeddings and perhaps the positional signal.

7. Mental analogy  
   Imagine you are editing a paragraph. For every word you pause and rapidly scan the whole paragraph, highlighting bits that matter for understanding this word (agreement, reference, theme). You do this with several highlighters at once (multi-head). Then you rewrite the word with all highlights in view. Repeat the pass several times—each pass refines everyone’s representation. That iterative global “group discussion” is what stacked self-attention layers emulate.

8. Typical life of a sentence in a Transformer (encoder only, e.g. BERT)  
   “The sheriff awarded the deputy a medal.”  
   Step 0: Tokenize → vectors + positions  
   Layer 1: One head learns subject-verb agreement, another learns prepositional links, etc.  
   Layer 6: The ‘sheriff’ vector now encodes not just the word’s meaning but also its role (agent, authority, etc.), influenced by “awarded” and “medal.”  
   Final: A classifier atop the [CLS] vector predicts entailment, sentiment, etc.

9. What about math? (quick summary)  
   For one head:  
     Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V          (X: L×d input, W: d×d_k)  
     Attention = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)        (L×L matrix)  
     Output = Attention · V                 (L×d_k)  
   Multi-head = concat(head₁, …, head_h) W_O.

10. Caveats & evolutions  
    • The L² cost for long sequences spurred variants (Linformer, Performer, Longformer, etc.) that approximate attention or truncate it.  
    • Positional encoding choices are now a design space (sinusoidal, learned, rotary, relative, etc.).  
    • The Transformer block itself is being tweaked (e.g., Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm, parallel vs serial attention/MLP, gating).

In one sentence  

A Transformer repeatedly lets every token softly search the whole sequence for relevant information (self-attention), collects that information in several complementary ways (multi-head), mixes and refines it with per-token MLPs, and—thanks to residual connections and massive parallel matrix ops—builds powerful, scalable representations that drive today’s state-of-the-art models in language, vision, and beyond.
